title: The ruined novel
sentences: With full spirits, his heart filled with the mysterious murmur of spring and the skylark's gaiety, he left Kecskemét and, having looked up Lőrinc Tóth in Pest,
who invited him for a glass of Rác wine in a tavern in Buda where actors also came and went,
the next day he set out for home by boat with the firm resolve that he would become a notary in Komárom, as his father had commanded.
As soon as he had rested from the journey's fatigue at his mother's and at the Válys',
he savoured to the full the joys of reunion and entered service as a legal clerk with Mr. István Asztalos, Komárom's most popular advocate.
Not much jurisprudence lingered in his head, nor much inclination for it—but what was he to do?
Painting or literature, between which his inclination wavered, were not yet careers in those days.
Perhaps they still are not in Hungary—but then they brought nothing to the table; they were amusements fit for the rich.
He received no pay from Asztalos, but Asztalos did not wish him to bend his back at the writing desk.
It was enough if he gained a little scent of the practical side of the profession: how justice is seized and turned,
how one must deal with judges and how with clients.
Mr. Móric did not exert himself overmuch; he appeared at one or two hearings and sometimes looked in at the office.
As a curiosity he drafted a petition or contract, which Mr. Asztalos crossed out and corrected—a proceeding that fairly dampened his spirits—
otherwise he lived his favourite occupation, scribbled, and even painted at Gábor Orbán's lodging a picture of a castle, quite shut away, as good as without companions.
Brought here from the air of Kecskemét, he became once more the old shunner of company.
At home in the Szombati Street house he did not feel at ease during the day.
That was not loneliness.
The house consisted of three living rooms, apart from a butcher's shop and some outbuildings, but for part of the year Károly Jókay,
the present "father of orphans," also lived here, only for short intervals, spending the summer on his estate at Ekel, which he had received with his wife.
The Válys lived in Kapitány Street, but they spent much of the day with the old lady,
so the house was nearly filled by the family alone; to this was added a great deal of visiting.
Sometimes on summer afternoons not everyone could fit into the rooms—the knitting aunts crowded together.
The corridor filled up too, which was otherwise finer than the rooms, with its six red marble columns.
To every guest Mrs. Jókay explained a hundred times that she loved the columns because her little Móric in his schoolboy days had learned his lesson
by pacing around one of the columns, turning right and left, until at last the task entered his head.
Móric therefore could not have a separate room here and consequently scarcely stayed at home; he rose in the early morning hours and, after breakfast,
went out to their garden on the island, where he practised the gymnastics he had come to love in Kecskemét, on the horizontal bar and with weights, according to Uncle Iványos, the family doctor.
Meanwhile he continued his novel begun in Kecskemét, "Weekdays," wandering in spirit over the endless plains of the Alföld.
When he grew tired of writing, he exercised again or sank into silent wonder at nature.
At the midday bell his mother sent lunch here; if something good had been baked or cooked in the Válys' kitchen,
Eszter sent some too; sometimes he had to eat two lunches, and then much went to Lakőr, the Válys' dog,
who, having grasped the situation, to Jókai's great amusement, sided with whoever brought the lunch.
[33] The afternoon he spent then just as the morning, and he was almost vexed, could not find his place, if toward evening the family members went out and disturbed him.
Thus he lived until the heart of autumn arrived; he came in the dark, went in the dark, so that the gentry of Komárom wondered continually,
hearing how tall and handsome a young man he had become, yet no one had even seen him.
The ladies of the town already jested that perhaps Mrs. Jókay kept young Móric—like a sheltered maiden—locked in the cellar, lest the town should spirit him away.
The sharp autumn weather, however, at last drove him into town, where he could work only slowly on finishing "Weekdays."
Around Christmas it was ready, and now he too could throw himself into the winter pleasures, at least insofar as they suited his taste.
He had indeed gained much confidence in Kecskemét and, like his father once, had grown into a very pleasant figure in society.
At name-days, which followed inexhaustibly among the friends of the Jókay house, Móric began to be the universal entertainer.
Right after Christmas these great festivities got under way.
And they began with the rectory.
The bishop, Mihály Nagy, held a name-day for his wife, Ágnes Thaly.
There was a daughter in the house too, the lovely Lina Püspök, who with great fondness brought the blushing Móric to confusion with her playful teasing.
Miss Lina liked that he fled from her, wherefore she pressed her attentions upon him in company.
At Paul's turn it was name-day at the Nagy Páls', at Charles's evening Károly Jókay gave a banquet,
on Francis's day at the Vály Ferencs', on the day of the Blessed Virgin's betrothal, likewise in carnival season, widow Mrs. Jókay held Maria's day grandly at her own house.
Of course these revels begot new revels again, and Móric was now indispensable,
not only because he was the handsomest and most promising youth in Komárom at that time, but because a thousand uses could be made of him.
Already in that no one could cut such beautiful paper lace under the cakes with scissors
as he, so that they had to be admired like works of art.
Besides, he became such a csárdás dancer in the "famous town" that tears gathered in the old men's eyes when they watched.
And how beautifully he could recite!
And with what inventiveness he arranged the then fashionable parlour games, whose essence was pawn redemption!
At nearly every name-day eve he invented a new parlour game and a new method of pawn redemption for "I Fell into the Well."
In this year and at these Komárom name-day eves those were first performed, and from here they spread elsewhere.
He invented "Bringing Down the Starry Sky," "the Endless Tree,"
"the Mourning of the Spanish King," "the Fan-Ship Arriving from Holland," "How Do You Like It?" and the like.
[34] This renewed Móric knew everything that impresses at such gatherings, as though he were already here casting in advance a hero of his own later novels.
While he thus amused himself, he smoothed his first novel; in life, too, a first romance began to weave itself.
Among the figures of the described festivities one of the most graceful was the lovely lily-faced, raven-haired, airy Etelka Asztalos,
who most often chose Móric as her dance partner and, wherever she appeared thereafter, by that wireless telegraphy
which has existed between the youth of both sexes since time immemorial, betrayed to observers that she cherished tender feelings toward Móric.
Móric noticed this too and secretly shared them, but since Móric was even more maiden-like than Etelka, he better preserved an air of indifference.
Though before the knitting aunts' Argus eyes nothing is secret.
Those tiny sparks had to flare up more and more, for there were many points of contact.
Móric had a convenient excuse for visiting the Asztaloses, as Mr. Asztalos's articled clerk,
and Etelka similarly had reason to call daily at the Válys', for she took lessons from the professor in history and natural history.
When the lesson was over, Móric too came to the "in-laws," at first by chance, later by design.
Etelka, as though exchanged, turned from white to red as Móric entered, and Móric, once he had fought through the first awkwardness,
a struggle that renewed itself day by day, was seized by a wondrous volubility such as usually springs from rapture.
Good Eszter, Mrs. Vály, with feminine delicacy soon noticed the budding idyll and, leaving the young people to talk a little,
always finished with the instruction: "Go, my dear Móric, escort Etelka home!" And Móric never needed to be told twice.
Though the following spring, in the very days of March, he moved to Pest
to prepare for the bar examination, he often journeyed back to Komárom; the memory of the lovely girl drew him there.
Sometimes he came for only a day, but he stayed home for two weeks under various pretexts;
once he brought Petőfi with him, whose resonant name was already known throughout the country.
On this occasion Petőfi lodged with the Válys, because the guest room—Mrs. Jókay's "clean room"—was already occupied,
but the worthy lady's care extended even here to her son's guest, and she filled his room overnight with wine bottles.
She was greatly surprised that Petőfi drank none of them, and even more surprised when Petőfi scolded her in the morning.
"You thought, did you not, dear lady, that whoever writes those ballads must surely love wine?"
Petőfi, whose unusual dress—a dark-green dolman woven through with coloured flowers, brown velvet Hungarian trousers, and tasselled top-boots—caused great sensation in the town,
stayed in Komárom only one day, and he too found Etelka beautiful.
Perhaps he had come precisely to see her—if indeed Móric poured out his soul to him, which, knowing his character, is hard to suppose.
Móric stayed a week this time too, and thereafter he almost every week hurried home and escorted Etelka from her lessons.
In the town people had already begun to whisper about the handsome, well-matched pair, when suddenly, like lightning, Mrs. Asztalos's little letter struck down,
which arrived for Vály instead of Etelka and informed the professor that Etelka's parents considered her upbringing complete as of this day.
And so that there might be even more talk of it, a few days later Mrs. Asztalos travelled to the baths with her daughter.
Disappointed Móric, who sadly and now finally travelled back to Pest, could not discover
whence came the first frost that nipped these spring buds, only later, under another sky, where other flowers grew,
did it gradually become clear that the usual destroyer of small-town affairs, gossip, had ruined this well-begun relationship.
The chief culprit was Mrs. Jókay herself, who yet loved every member of the Asztalos family with her whole heart.
A hundred, a thousand times she will repent of it in the hours of bitterness that are to come.
The whole thing happened thus: someone mentioned the drifting rumour to her and even praised what a lovely daughter-in-law she would have.
"Never!" Mrs. Jókay burst out.
"While I live, I will not allow my son to marry a Catholic girl."
Nimble tongues told Mrs. Asztalos, and Mrs. Asztalos did not swallow it; she sent a message that Mrs. Jókay could not politely ignore,
whereupon Mrs. Jókay sent a reply, and thus over one lightly tossed remark good relations between the two families soured, and two lives took a different shape—
or rather only one, for the lovely Miss Asztalos languished, wasted away, came home ill in the autumn from the baths, and within a few days she died.
